blocks.content: Tribunals offer a speedier, less expensive, and more flexible system of justice, guided by the principles of natural justice rather than rigid procedural laws.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Tribunals offer flexibility in procedure as they are not bound by the rigid rules of the Civil Procedure Code (1908) or the Indian Evidence Act (1872).
They are guided primarily by the principles of natural justice, ensuring fair, informal, and rapid dispute resolution.
Tribunals combine judicial experience with administrative and technical expertise, enabling well-informed decisions in specialized sectors.
By diverting specific domain matters away from ordinary courts, tribunals reduce legal expenses and significantly alleviate judicial arrears.

rows: Strictly bound by Code of Civil Procedure and Evidence Act
Guided by Principles of Natural Justice; flexible procedure
Presided over exclusively by judicial officers
Composed of judicial members alongside technical/administrative experts
Designed for rapid, inexpensive, and informal dispute resolution
General civil jurisdiction over all civil suits
Specialized jurisdiction over specific matters (e.g., service matters, tax, environment)

items: Article 323A allows administrative tribunals to be established ONLY by Parliament, whereas Article 323B allows tribunals for other matters to be created by both Parliament and State Legislatures.
Under the L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997), the Supreme Court ruled that decisions of administrative tribunals are subject to judicial review by the High Court under Articles 226 and 227.
Tribunals are hybrid bodies containing both judicial members and administrative/technical experts.
